note: A host who had stolen money from his guests had lentils left on his mustache because he had not washed after eating. The guests went to his wife, said her husband had told them to ask her to return their money, and offered as proof that he had eaten lentils that day. She believed them and gave it back. In his anger, the husband divorced her.
why: Rav Dimi is teaching what can happen when people skip washing their hands before and after a meal; this is his case for washing after. Ravin then reports a harsher version in which the husband killed his wife.

terms.meaning: Washing the hands (and here the mouth) after a meal, as the Sages required.
Washing the hands before a meal.

flag: The Hebrew is a single line saying that neglecting the final waters led to a divorce; the incident itself appears only in the translator's explanation.

note: Levi visited the house of Yosef the bird hunter, where he was served a peacock's head cooked in milk, and he said nothing to them. When Levi came before Rabbi, Rabbi asked him why he had not excommunicated them. Levi answered that the town was the locale of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, and he thought Rabbi Yehuda might have taught them as Rabbi Yosei HaGelili did, that birds are excluded because they have no mother's milk.
why: The Gemara has just shown that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili left birds out of the ban on meat with milk, and that his own town ate poultry cooked in milk; Levi's silence shows a visitor respecting a town that follows its own teacher's ruling.

people.name: Levi

people.name: Yosef the bird hunter
people.about: The host who served the dish.

people.name: Rabbi

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira

terms.meaning: To place someone under a ban that cuts him off from the community, a penalty for defying the Sages.
The Torah forbids cooking a kid in its mother's milk; the Sages debated whether this covers birds, which give no milk.
